newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Intrawest acquires Copper Mountain, Whistler.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Intrawest acquires Copper Mountain, Whistler.

text.p: In a bid to lead the rapidly consolidating North American ski industry, Canadian resort developer Intrawest Corp. announced a C$260 million (US$192 million) deal Wednesday to acquire Copper Mountain in Colorado and Whistler Mountain in British Columbia.

Intrawest will issue 6.1 million shares to the families that own the two independent resorts, representing a stake of about 20.9 percent. The shares were valued at around C$118 million (US$87 million) based on Intrawest's stock price of C$19.35 before the announcement.
Intrawest will also assume about C$140 million (US$104 million) in debt with the final terms being determined when the deal closes in March.
The moves "position Intrawest to emerge as the leader in the ongoing consolidation of the North American ski resort industry," said Intrawest President Joe Houssian.

The company will own eight mountain resorts ranging from Stratton, Vermont to Blackcomb in British Columbia and is closing in on its biggest competitor -- Vail Resorts Inc. in Colorado which is seeking to buy three nearby resorts from Ralcorp Holdings Inc. for US$300 million.

Intrawest said its combined operations receive about 4.6 million skier visits a year, with about 1.7 million of those coming from the new operations. The expanded Vail gets about 5 million skiier visits annually.

Intrawest projected the acquisitions would immediately increase its earnings and cash flow per share, although the company declined to quantify the size of the gain. Intrawest had earnings of C$18.8 million (US$13.9 million) on revenues of C$283.3 million (US$210 million) in its fiscal year ended June 30.
Investors applauded Wednesday's announcement and Intrawest shares shot to a new year high of C$20.90 (US$15.48) on the Toronto Stock Exchange, a gain of C$1.55 (US$1.15).
"It's a signficant positive for the company. They have been looking for a solid resort in the Colorado area for some time and it looks like Copper is it," said Salman Partners analyst Kevin Eldridge.

Copper, about 75 miles (120 km) west of Denver, operates under a 40-year permit from the U.S. Forest Service and is owned by a family investment group headed by Tony Novelly of St. Louis. It was one of the last remaining independent ski resorts in Colorado.

Whistler, located about 75 miles (120 km) north of Vancouver, is adjacent to Intrawest's Blackomb mountain operation and the two have consistently been rated by skiing magazines as one of the premier resorts in North America.
Whistler was founded in 1966 and has been owned by the Young and Barker families for 17 years.

Intrawest said it would invest C$70 million (US$52 million) in ski-operation expansion at Copper and Whistler and spend C$460 million (US$340 million) on real-estate development at the base of Copper over 10 years.

Intrawest made it clear it was still hunting for other resort acquisitions, citing Utah and northern California as areas of interest. Houssian also expressed a desire to buy a summer-oriented, beach or desert resort with a focus on golf.
"We have not hit the parameters of our strategic growth plan," he said.

Intrawest said the catalyst for Wednesday's deal was the recent mergers of other industry operators which has left two major competitors -- Vail and American Skiing Co. Intrawest needed to grow to ensure its ability to compete while Whistler and Copper realized they needed to join with a bigger operator to gain capital and expertise.
"There's tremendous consolidation going on...Reality is setting in. It's becoming a more sophisticated business," said Houssian.
Wednesday's news followed a C$250 million ($185 million) deal by Intrawest earlier this month to build a resort village at the base of Squaw Peak in Lake Tahoe, California.

Intrawest, which was a diverse real-estate concern until deciding in 1994 to focus solely on resorts, also announced Wednesday it will issue a new class of special stock to represent its remaining C$86 million (US$64 million) of non-resort properties. Those assets are slated for sale over the next four years with proceeds being paid out to shareholders.
